relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 4 years
decision_summary: Commission held that insurer failed to prove the policyholder had prior knowledge or diagnosis of diabetes before policy inception; mere post-hoc lab values were insufficient to establish non-disclosure.
successful_arguments: No documented diagnosis or treatment for diabetes existed before the policy start date
Insurer relied only on a single post-hospitalization lab report to infer a pre-existing condition, which the commission found insufficient
Policyholder had disclosed all conditions known to them at the time of application
key_evidence: Pre-policy medical records showing no diabetes diagnosis
Proposal form copy showing accurate disclosure of known conditions
Treating doctor's certificate on date of first diagnosis
source_citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Maharashtra, Consumer Case (illustrative, verify before public use)
regulation_sources: IRDAI Circular IRDA/HLT/REG/CIR/059/03/2017 — burden of proof for non-disclosure lies with insurer

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 4 years
decision_summary: Insurer's own empanelled doctor's pre-policy medical check-up report did not flag diabetes; commission held insurer cannot repudiate on a condition its own underwriting process missed.
successful_arguments: Insurer's pre-issuance medical examination did not detect or record diabetes
Burden of proof for non-disclosure lies with insurer and was not discharged
key_evidence: Insurer's own pre-policy medical examination report
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Karnataka (illustrative, verify before public use)
regulation_sources: IRDAI Protection of Policyholders' Interests Regulations 2017, Regulation 8

relevant_policy_clause: PED exclusion clause, waiting period 3 years
decision_summary: Commission found clear documentary evidence (prior prescription records dated before policy inception) that policyholder was aware of and being treated for diabetes but did not disclose it in the proposal form.
failed_arguments: Policyholder argued they were unaware of the diagnosis, but pre-policy pharmacy records and a treating physician's prescription pre-dating the policy contradicted this
Argument that the condition was 'mild and unremarkable' did not overcome the non-disclosure finding
key_evidence: Pre-policy prescription dated 8 months before policy inception, explicitly for diabetes management
source_citation: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (illustrative, verify before public use)

relevant_policy_clause: 2-year waiting period for joint replacement surgery
decision_summary: Waiting period clause was validly applied and upheld, but commission directed partial payment for the portion of treatment (diagnostics, medication) not directly tied to the excluded surgical procedure.
successful_arguments: Ancillary treatment costs unrelated to the specific excluded procedure should be assessed separately
failed_arguments: Argument that the waiting period clause itself was unconscionable was rejected — it was clearly disclosed and IRDAI-compliant
key_evidence: Itemized hospital bill separating surgical and non-surgical costs
Policy document with waiting period schedule
source_citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Tamil Nadu (illustrative, verify before public use)
regulation_sources: IRDAI Health Insurance Regulations 2016, Regulation 11 — Waiting period provisions

relevant_policy_clause: Clause 7 — Claim intimation and document submission requirements
decision_summary: Ombudsman found insurer had raised document deficiencies in piecemeal fashion over multiple communications rather than issuing a single consolidated deficiency notice as required by IRDAI regulations. Claim upheld in full.
successful_arguments: Insurer violated the single consolidated deficiency notice requirement under IRDAI Circular IRDA/HLT/MISC/CIR/216/09/2020
Policyholder submitted all documents requested in the first deficiency letter within the stipulated time
Subsequent additional document requests were made after the permitted response window, precluding rejection on documentation grounds
key_evidence: Timeline of insurer's document request communications showing piecemeal requests
Courier receipts and acknowledgments proving timely submission of each batch
Hospital-certified duplicate bills and discharge summary
source_citation: Office of the Insurance Ombudsman, Kolkata (illustrative, verify before public use)
regulation_sources: IRDAI Circular IRDA/HLT/MISC/CIR/216/09/2020 — Health insurance claim processing timelines
IRDAI Protection of Policyholders' Interests Regulations 2017, Regulation 9

relevant_policy_clause: Exclusion — obesity treatment and weight management procedures
decision_summary: Ombudsman directed partial settlement covering the medically necessary component of the bariatric surgery (60%) due to life-threatening comorbidities (hypertension, sleep apnea), while the elective weight-loss component remained excluded under the policy.
successful_arguments: Surgery was medically necessary to treat covered comorbidities — not purely elective
Treating physician's letter explicitly stated life-threatening comorbidity risk
Policy exclusion clause did not explicitly exclude medically necessary bariatric surgery for covered conditions
IRDAI circular on medically necessary treatment overrides blanket exclusion
failed_arguments: Claim for full amount rejected — elective weight-loss component remained excluded
key_evidence: Treating physician's medical necessity certificate citing hypertension and sleep apnea
Pre-surgery test reports showing critical comorbidity levels
source_citation: Office of the Insurance Ombudsman, Mumbai (illustrative, verify before public use)
regulation_sources: IRDAI Circular IRDAI/HLT/MISC/CIR/245/11/2019 — Medically necessary treatment coverage
Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017, Rule 16 — Partial relief orders
